title: Microsoft Fabric Capacity: Units, SKUs, Bursting, Throttling, and Sizing
summary: A comprehensive practitioner reference covering every verified aspect of Microsoft Fabric capacity: how capacity units (CUs) are defined, the F SKU ladder, licensing thresholds, Spark vCore mapping, warehouse smoothing, the four-stage throttling model, burndown mechanics, workload-specific exceptions, and operational constraints including private-link provisioning delays.
body_md:
## What Is a Fabric Capacity and Why Does It Matter?

Microsoft Fabric is a unified SaaS analytics platform, but "unified" does not mean "free-form." Every workload — notebooks, warehouses, pipelines, semantic models, real-time streams — draws compute from a single shared pool called a **capacity**. Understanding how that pool is measured, purchased, and governed is the single most consequential operational decision a Fabric practitioner makes.

A capacity is a dedicated pool of resources that performs work in Fabric [S2]. All operations, regardless of workload type, are measured in a single unit: **capacity units (CUs)**. Every request draws CUs from the available capacity, and consumption is classified as either an *interactive* operation (user-facing, latency-sensitive) or a *background* operation (batch, long-running) [S2]. This two-class model underpins every throttling and smoothing decision the platform makes.

Fabric enforces throttling at the capacity level, not at the tenant level [S6]. If one capacity becomes saturated, only the workspaces assigned to it are affected; other capacities in the same tenant continue operating normally [S6]. This isolation property makes capacity boundaries a first-class architectural boundary — one you can use deliberately to isolate critical workloads from experimental or bursty ones.

---

## The SKU Ladder and Capacity Units

Fabric F SKUs run from F2 up to F2048 [S1]. The SKU number is not arbitrary: it equals the number of CUs the capacity provides. An F64 supplies exactly 64 CUs, and each step up the ladder doubles the compute of the previous tier [S1]. The doubling relationship means sizing decisions are binary — there is no "F96" between F64 and F128 — so headroom planning matters.

Microsoft is consolidating purchase options around F SKUs and retiring the older Power BI Premium per-capacity P SKUs. The documentation maps F64 to the former P1 (8 v-cores) for rough compute comparison only, not licensing equivalence [S1]. Practitioners transitioning from P-SKU tenants should treat the mapping as directional, not exact.

### The F64 Licensing Threshold

F64 carries a specific licensing significance beyond its compute size. On an F64 or larger capacity, users holding only a free Fabric license can view Power BI content when they have a workspace viewer role [S1]. On smaller F SKUs — F2 through F32 — every viewer needs a Pro or Premium Per User (PPU) license [S1]. A capacity is also required to use Copilot; neither a Pro nor a PPU license alone enables Copilot features [S3].

### Trial Capacity

The Fabric trial grants a capacity equivalent to an F64 for 60 days [S1]. It behaves like F64 for Power BI viewing rights, making it a realistic sandbox for evaluating all Fabric experiences before purchase [S1]. The trial is not a reduced preview — it is a full F64 equivalent, so performance observations made during a trial are meaningful for production sizing decisions.

---

## Shared Capacity and Workspace Assignment

Every Fabric-enabled tenant includes a **shared capacity** that hosts all personal My Workspaces plus Pro and PPU workspace types [S1]. New workspaces land on this shared capacity by default and can later be reassigned to any capacity in the tenant [S1]. The shared capacity is not metered the same way as F SKU capacities — it exists to support free and Pro users but does not provide the performance isolation, burst headroom, or Azure-integration features of a dedicated F SKU.

Workspaces on Fabric F SKUs gain Azure-integration capabilities not available on the shared capacity, including ARM APIs, Terraform support, and managed private endpoints [S1]. These capabilities matter when architecting for infrastructure-as-code deployment pipelines or private networking.

---

## How CUs Translate to Workload Resources

### Spark vCores

The conversion from CUs to Spark compute is explicit and documented. Each Fabric CU grants two Spark vCores, and a 3x burst multiplier applies on top [S4]. An F64 SKU therefore exposes up to 384 Spark vCores (64 CU × 2 × 3), which sets the ceiling for how large a custom Spark pool can be configured [S4].

*Inference:* The 3x burst multiplier means that an F64's sustained Spark compute (128 vCores without burst) is meaningfully different from its peak burst compute (384 vCores). Sizing exercises that assume peak vCores without accounting for burst duration may overestimate sustained throughput.

### Direct Lake Memory Bounds

The capacity SKU sets the maximum memory available to each Direct Lake semantic model, which bounds how much column data can be resident at once [S7]. Larger SKUs allow more column data to remain in memory, reducing the frequency of cold-read fallbacks. *Inference:* For large Direct Lake models, SKU selection is partly a memory sizing decision, not only a compute one.

### Warehouse Smoothing

Warehouse workloads explicitly benefit from burstable capacity and smoothing [S5]. Smoothing spreads the evaluation of compute consumption over time so spiky peak-time usage is offset against idle periods [S5]. This means a warehouse that runs a heavy load at midnight pays down that cost gradually across subsequent timepoints rather than being immediately throttled.

---

## Bursting and Smoothing: The Core Mechanics

Fabric uses two complementary mechanisms to handle variable workload intensity without penalising users for temporary spikes [S6]:

- **Bursting** lets an operation consume more CUs than the SKU's provisioned rate allows, so it completes quickly rather than being artificially slowed.
- **Smoothing** spreads the CU cost of that burst across future timepoints, allowing the capacity to "pay back" the debt over time.

### Timepoints and the 24-Hour Window

The fundamental unit of time in Fabric's capacity accounting is the **timepoint**, which is 30 seconds long [S6]. There are 2,880 timepoints in a 24-hour window [S6]. Smoothing does not charge the full CU cost at the moment an operation starts; instead, it distributes that cost across those future 30-second slices.

The smoothing window differs by operation class:

- **Interactive operations** are smoothed over a minimum of 5 minutes and up to 64 minutes, depending on total CU consumption [S6].
- **Background operations** are always smoothed over a full 24-hour window because they typically carry much larger CU loads [S6].

This design means a heavy overnight batch job (background) will have its cost spread across the following 2,880 timepoints, making it very unlikely to spike the capacity into throttling territory the next morning — unless the batch is enormous relative to the SKU size.

### Autoscale Billing Exception

Bursting and smoothing do not apply when a capacity admin has enabled Autoscale Billing for Spark [S6]. In that configuration, Spark usage operates in pay-as-you-go mode only, and the standard CU pool accounting no longer governs Spark jobs [S6].

---

## The Four-Stage Throttling Model

![Fabric capacity throttling and smoothing](/content/diagrams/capacity-throttling.svg)

Fabric's throttling system is staged progressively across four thresholds, keyed to how much **future capacity** has been pre-consumed by already-smoothed operations [S6]. The metric is not instantaneous CU usage — it is the aggregate of smoothed future commitments already on the books.

| Future Usage Consumed | Effect on Interactive Operations | Effect on Background Operations |
|---|---|---|
| Up to 10 minutes | No throttling (overage protection) | No throttling |
| 10 – 60 minutes | 20-second delay imposed on new submissions | No throttling |
| 60 minutes – 24 hours | Outright rejection | May still start |
| Beyond 24 hours | Rejected | Rejected |

[S6]

A few important clarifications:

**Operations in flight are protected.** Operations already executing when a capacity enters a throttling state are always allowed to run to completion; only new operation submissions are subject to delay or rejection [S6].

**Error surface.** When a capacity rejects requests, users receive HTTP status code `CapacityLimitExceeded` along with error messages indicating that compute capacity limits have been reached [S6].

**Classification can shift.** The throttling system classifies operations at submission time before execution begins. Classification can change once runtime information becomes available. In ambiguous cases the system defaults to the background classification, which favours the user by applying the more lenient 24-hour smoothing window [S6].

---

## Carryforward and Burndown: How Throttling Clears

Throttling is not a static state that requires manual intervention. It is governed by a running balance called **carryforward CUs**.

When accumulated future-capacity usage exceeds the 10-minute overage protection window, the excess is recorded as carryforward CUs [S6]. Each subsequent timepoint that has idle capacity reduces this carryforward balance through a process called **burndown** [S6]. Throttling enforcement continues until the full carryforward balance reaches zero [S6].

*Inference:* A capacity that has been running at sustained high utilisation will have a large carryforward balance. Even after workload intensity drops, the burndown process plays out over many timepoints (each timepoint is 30 seconds), so throttling can persist for minutes to hours after the triggering load ends. Practitioners who observe throttling "linger" after a busy period are seeing burndown in action, not a system bug.

---

## Workload-Specific Exceptions to Throttling

Three workload types behave differently from the standard throttling rules [S6]:

1. **Fabric Eventstreams** reduce allocated CU resources rather than delaying or rejecting new stream operations when a capacity is under pressure. The stream continues but at reduced capacity allocation.

2. **Real-Time Intelligence (RTI)** skips the 20-second interactive delay stage entirely and only begins throttling at the 60-minute rejection threshold. RTI is designed for latency-sensitive workloads, so the intermediate delay stage would defeat its purpose.

3. **Warehouse operations** are classified as background operations to benefit from 24-hour smoothing. However, a background operation triggered by an interactive chain (for example, a user report that triggers a warehouse query that triggers a pipeline) can be promoted to interactive throttling rules [S6].

### Compound Throttling Protection

Fabric provides compound throttling protection so that a single end-user request that fans out into a chain of dependent operations — for example, a report visual querying a semantic model that reads from OneLake — is throttled at most once per capacity in the chain [S6]. The platform prevents the same request from being penalised multiple times as it traverses cross-workload dependencies [S6].

---

## SKU Capabilities Beyond Compute

### Embedding

Power BI Embedded A SKUs and EM SKUs support only Power BI items, not Fabric items [S1]. Embedding architectures that also require lakehouses, warehouses, notebooks, or other Fabric workloads must pair the embedding surface with an F capacity [S1].

### Private Networking

Provisioning a new capacity while tenant-level private links are active can take up to 24 hours to propagate into the private DNS zone [S8]. The tenant-level private link configuration also blocks tenant migrations entirely for the duration it is enabled [S8]. Both constraints are operationally significant: capacity additions during a private-link-enabled window must be planned with DNS propagation lag in mind, and tenants considering a migration cannot do so while tenant-level private links are active.

---

## Best Practices

These are derived from pattern-type verified claims.

**Align capacity boundaries to isolation requirements.** Because throttling is enforced at the capacity level rather than the tenant level [S6], separate capacities provide genuine compute isolation. Place workloads with strict SLAs on a dedicated capacity rather than sharing with bursty or experimental workloads.

**Use the F64 threshold deliberately for licensing.** If your organisation's report consumers do not have Pro licenses, sizing to at least F64 enables free-license viewers [S1]. Sizing to F32 or below requires every viewer to hold a Pro or PPU license, which changes the total cost of ownership calculation.

**Treat background operations as the safe default for batch.** Background operations receive 24-hour smoothing [S6], meaning large batch loads are far less likely to trigger throttling than interactive operations of equivalent CU cost. Ensure pipelines, warehouse loads, and other scheduled jobs are correctly classified as background.

**Plan capacity provisioning lag under private links.** If tenant-level private links are enabled, schedule capacity provisioning at least 24 hours before workloads need the new capacity [S8].

**Account for the 3x Spark burst ceiling when sizing pools.** The maximum pool size is bounded by CU × 2 × 3 vCores [S4]. Do not configure a custom Spark pool that exceeds the available burst vCores for the SKU — the configuration will be capped at the SKU limit.

---

## What Goes Wrong

### Confusing PPU with Fabric Capacity

Relying on Power BI Premium Per User (PPU) licenses to run Fabric workloads is a design mistake [S1]. PPU is a per-user feature set, not a capacity. It cannot create or run non-Power BI Fabric items such as lakehouses, warehouses, or notebooks — an F SKU or Trial capacity is required for those workloads [S1].

### Assuming Throttling Clears Immediately

Throttling persists until the carryforward balance burns down to zero [S6]. Teams that schedule a second large batch immediately after a throttled first batch will find the second batch also throttled, because the burndown from the first batch is still in progress. Stagger heavy background loads to allow burndown between runs.

### Treating Shared Capacity as a Staging Environment

The shared capacity hosts My Workspaces and Pro/PPU workspaces but does not provide the isolation, burst headroom, or Azure-integration features of an F SKU [S1]. Using shared capacity as a development or staging environment can produce results that do not reflect production F SKU behavior.

### Missing the Autoscale Exception for Spark

When Autoscale Billing for Spark is enabled, the standard bursting and smoothing mechanics do not apply to Spark [S6]. Teams that enable Autoscale Billing expecting the standard smoothing protection for Spark workloads will be surprised by pay-as-you-go billing behavior.

---

## Performance and Internals

This section covers the L4-depth verified claims — the mechanics that underpin observable capacity behavior.

### Timepoint Arithmetic

Every CU accounting calculation in Fabric runs at 30-second timepoint granularity [S6]. With 2,880 timepoints per 24-hour window [S6], the system maintains a rolling 24-hour view of committed future CU obligations. Each new operation submission adds its smoothed CU cost to future timepoints; each completed timepoint with spare capacity reduces the carryforward balance.

### Interactive vs. Background Smoothing Windows

The asymmetry between the interactive smoothing window (5–64 minutes) and the background smoothing window (24 hours) [S6] has a direct implication for burst capacity planning:

- An interactive operation that consumes a large CU burst will spread its cost over at most 64 minutes — 128 timepoints. If the capacity's CU provision is already committed during that 128-timepoint window, the next interactive operations face throttling.
- A background operation of identical CU cost spreads over 2,880 timepoints. The per-timepoint increment is approximately 22 times smaller, making it far less likely to push future-usage totals past any throttling threshold.

### Throttling State Machine

The throttling model is best understood as a state machine driven by a single variable: accumulated future CU obligations as a fraction of the SKU's per-timepoint provision [S6].

1. **Clean state** (future obligations < 10 minutes of provision): full throughput, no restrictions.
2. **Overage state** (10–60 minutes): interactive submissions receive a 20-second delay, background is unaffected.
3. **Rejection state** (60 minutes – 24 hours): interactive submissions are rejected outright; background operations may still start depending on remaining headroom.
4. **Full rejection** (> 24 hours): all new submissions rejected, regardless of classification.

Transitions between states happen at each timepoint boundary as carryforward is either added (by new operations) or reduced (by idle capacity burning down) [S6].

### Classification Ambiguity and the Background Default

The throttling classifier runs at submission time, before the operation executes [S6]. When Fabric cannot determine whether an operation will be interactive or background — which can happen for operations triggered by system processes or orchestration chains — it defaults to background classification [S6]. This default is user-friendly: background classification applies the longer smoothing window, reducing the chance of immediate throttling. Once runtime information resolves the ambiguity, the classification can be updated [S6].

### Compound Throttling Architecture

Compound throttling protection [S6] requires the platform to track request lineage across workload boundaries. When a report visual triggers a semantic model query that in turn triggers an OneLake read, the platform attributes that entire chain to a single originating request. The throttle-once-per-capacity guarantee prevents multiplicative throttling on fan-out query patterns — a critical safeguard for report-driven architectures where a single user action can generate dozens of downstream compute operations.

---

## Worked Example: Sizing an F64 for a Mixed Workload

Consider a team planning an F64 capacity to support the following workloads:

- **Interactive reports** served from Direct Lake semantic models (user-facing, business hours)
- **Nightly warehouse loads** (batch, background)
- **Spark notebooks** for data transformation (mixed, depends on scheduling)

Sizing decisions ultimately come down to three branching questions — scale up the SKU, enable Autoscale Billing for Spark, or split workloads across capacities — each converging on the same checklist of limits below.

![Original diagram: Fabric capacity sizing decision tree - when to scale up the SKU, enable Autoscale Billing for Spark, or split workloads across capacities, with a sizing checklist covering Spark vCore ceilings, Direct Lake memory bounds, and the F64 licensing threshold](/diagrams/capacity-sku-decision.svg)

**Step 1 — Spark vCore budget.** An F64 provides 64 CUs × 2 × 3 = 384 burst Spark vCores [S4]. Sustained (non-burst) is 128 vCores. If the Spark notebooks run during business hours simultaneously with interactive reports, they compete for the same CU pool.

**Step 2 — Licensing.** At F64, free-license users can view reports in workspaces where they hold a viewer role [S1]. This is the breakeven point for broad report distribution without Pro license costs.

**Step 3 — Throttling exposure.** The nightly warehouse load is background-classified and smoothed over 24 hours [S5][S6]. *Inference:* If the load runs from 00:00 to 02:00, its CU cost is spread across 2,880 timepoints starting at midnight. By 08:00 business hours, approximately one-third of the smoothed cost will have been charged. If the warehouse load is very large relative to the F64 provision, it could push the capacity toward the overage or rejection state during early morning hours, delaying the first interactive reports of the day.

**Step 4 — Direct Lake memory.** The F64 SKU sets the memory ceiling for Direct Lake models [S7]. If the semantic models are large, the SKU's memory bound determines how much column data stays warm. *Inference:* A large Direct Lake model that regularly exceeds the F64 memory bound will fall back to cold reads from OneLake, increasing query latency during peak hours.

**Step 5 — Mitigation.** Scheduling the warehouse batch to complete well before business hours allows the burndown process to reduce carryforward CUs before interactive traffic begins. Separating the Spark transformation jobs onto a dedicated capacity (or enabling Autoscale Billing for Spark) isolates their CU consumption from the interactive and warehouse workloads.
